title: Counting the Omer
hookLine: Jews count seven weeks of days from Passover to Shavuot, some giving each day a quality

lines: TODAY IS ONE DAY OF THE OMER.
cards: During Passover, in Jewish homes and synagogues, someone says a blessing in the evening and then one short sentence: today is one day of the Omer. The next evening: today is two days of the Omer. Then three.
Then four. A number said out loud, and nothing else to do. No meal attached to it, no special clothes.
Just the number, growing, all the way to the festival of Shavuot. And yet it has its own blessing, its own rules, and an old question about what happens if you forget.

teach.b: The count comes straight from the Torah.

Leviticus says, in the King James wording: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete."
That sheaf is the omer, an offering of new grain from the harvest. Seven weeks of days, counted one by one, then a festival: Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks. Passover remembers leaving Egypt.
Shavuot, tradition says, remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai. So the count walks a road, from being set free to being given something to live by.

teach.h: A COUNT UP, NOT A COUNTDOWN.
teach.b: And it's a count up, not a countdown. A countdown treats the days in between as a waiting room. A count up adds each day to the total, so every one of them is kept.
Over time a second layer grew.

Some Jews, following the kabbalists, give each of the seven weeks a quality, starting with chesed, loving-kindness, and each day within the week a shade of those qualities: loving-kindness within loving-kindness, strength within loving-kindness.

Then the rabbis add a very human question: what about someone who forgets to count for a whole day? One well-known ruling says keep counting, but without the blessing. A missed night doesn't send anyone back to the start.

how: Jews who keep the count say a blessing each evening from the second night of Passover and then state the day's number of the Omer until Shavuot; some also reflect on a kabbalistic quality assigned to that day.

games.q: you've been counting the Omer every evening, and you realize you forgot yesterday entirely. what does one well-known ruling say?
o: start the whole count over from one.
keep counting, but without the blessing.
stop for this year and try again next year.
games.why: keep going. the blessing is left out, but the count goes on, all the way to Shavuot.

practice: Take the quality the count begins with, loving-kindness, and look for it in your last day: where it came easily, and where it stalled or went missing, without grading yourself.
Then say quietly inside, the way a counter would: today is one. If you pray, you can hold that day before God; if you don't, just hold it in your attention, breath by breath.

wordCard.voice: Counting the Omer. Seven weeks of days, counted aloud one by one from Passover to Shavuot, and for some, a quality for every day. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a sheaf, and a measure of grain; the offering the count is named for.

carryVoice: Your line: count the days. The count is too important to drop over one missed night. Until tomorrow.
